title: Ocular Myasthenia Gravis: The Great Mimicker
summary: A comprehensive guide to Ocular Myasthenia Gravis (OMG), an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder characterized by fatigable ptosis and ophthalmoplegia. This infographic covers the clinical pearls, diagnostic maneuvers, and evidence-based management for residents and fellows.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Ocular Myasthenia Gravis (OMG) is a localized form of Myasthenia Gravis (MG) affecting only the levator palpebrae superioris, orbicularis oculi, and extraocular muscles. It is an autoimmune Type II hypersensitivity reaction where antibodies block or destroy post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the motor end-plate.

branches: AChR Antibodies (80-90% in gMG; 50% in OMG)
MuSK Antibodies (Muscle-Specific Kinase) - Rare in pure OMG

sections.title: Clinical Hallmarks
content: Fatigability: Symptoms worse toward the end of the day or after prolonged use.
Variability: Symptoms change from hour to hour or day to day.
Ptosis: Often asymmetric; may shift from one eye to the other.
Diplopia: Does not follow a single cranial nerve pattern (Pseudo-internuclear ophthalmoplegia).
Orbicularis Weakness: Difficulty keeping eyes tightly closed against resistance.
Pupillary Sparing: The pupil is NEVER involved in MG.

sections.title: The Bedside Diagnostic Toolkit
content: 1. Ice Pack Test: Apply ice to ptotic lid for 2 mins. Improvement of >2mm is (+) due to inhibited acetylcholinesterase.
2. Cogan's Lid Twitch: Overshoot of the upper lid when shifting gaze from down to primary position.
3. Curtain Sign: Manually lifting the more ptotic lid causes the contralateral lid to droop (Hering's Law).
4. Sleep Test: 30 minutes of sleep in a dark room leads to transient resolution of ptosis/diplopia.
5. Enhanced Ptosis: Maintaining upgaze for 60 seconds triggers or worsens lid droop.

rows: Highly specific; risk of generalization if positive.
More common in females; often severe bulbar/respiratory involvement.
High association with Thymoma, especially in older patients.
Progressive, symmetric, lack of variability, 'Frozen Globe'.
Strength improves with exercise; associated with SCLC.

sections.title: Investigations & Workup
content: 1. Serology: AChR-Ab (Binding, Blocking, Modulating), MuSK-Ab.
2. Electrophysiology: Single-fiber EMG (SFEMG) is the gold standard (95%+ sensitivity).
3. Repetitive Nerve Stimulation (RNS): >10% decrement in amplitude.
4. Imaging: Chest CT or MRI to rule out Thymoma (Mandatory in all MG patients).
5. Thyroid Panel: Check TSH/T4 due to high co-occurrence of TED.

sections.title: Management Ladder
content: 1. First Line: Pyridostigmine (Mestinon) 60mg TID-QID. Adjust for symptoms.
2. Second Line: Corticosteroids (Prednisone). Start low/slow to avoid transient worsening.
3. Steroid Sparing: Azathioprine, Mycophenolate Mofetil, or Cyclosporine.
4. Crisis/Severe: IVIG or Plasmapheresis (PLEX).
5. Thymectomy: If thymoma present or in non-thymomatous gMG (MGTX trial).

sections.title: Red Flags & Contraindicated Drugs
content: MYASTHENIC CRISIS: Respiratory failure or severe dysphagia (Emergency!).
Avoid Fluoroquinolones (Ciprofloxacin/Levofloxacin) - can precipitate crisis.
Avoid Aminoglycosides (Gentamicin/Tobramycin).
Avoid Beta-blockers (Systemic and Topical Timolol).
Avoid Magnesium Sulfate.
Neuromuscular blockers (Succinylcholine/Vecuronium) require extreme caution in surgery.

rows: Mild generalized MG; slow progression; no crisis.
Moderate generalized MG; severe skeletal/bulbar involvement.
Acute fulminating MG; rapid onset; respiratory crisis.
Late severe MG; progression from Grade I/II.

content.explanation: S: Simpson's test (upgaze fatigue), T: Tensilon test (Edrophonium), A: Antibodies (AChR/MuSK), R: Rest (Ice pack/Sleep test), E: EMG (Single-fiber).

sections.title: Surgical Nuances
content: Ptosis Surgery: Generally avoided unless MG is medically stable for >1 year.
Sling vs. Levator Resection: Frontalis sling is often preferred due to poor levator function and risk of lagophthalmos.
Strabismus Surgery: Rarely performed due to the shifting nature of the deviation; prisms are first-line.
Pre-op Warning: Always notify anesthesiology about MG status due to sensitivity to paralytics.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: OMG patients with positive AChR antibodies are more likely to generalize.
The 'pseudointernuclear ophthalmoplegia' of MG can be distinguished from a true INO because MG lacks the nystagmus of the abducting eye.
Tensilon (Edrophonium) test is rarely used now due to risks of bradycardia/asystole; keep Atropine at bedside if performing.
Prednisone can cause a transient 'dip' in muscle strength during the first 7-10 days of therapy.

sections.title: Landmark Study: EPITOME & MGTX
sections.content: The MGTX Trial (2016) demonstrated that thymectomy plus prednisone was superior to prednisone alone in non-thymomatous gMG patients (ages 18-65) regarding symptom control and steroid-sparing. For pure OMG, the EPITOME trial explored low-dose steroids, suggesting earlier intervention may reduce the rate of generalization, though this remains a topic of clinical debate.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: 90% of those who generalize will do so within the first 2 years of onset.
If MG remains purely ocular for 3 years, the chance of generalization is <10%.
Exposure keratopathy: A common complication of ptosis surgery or severe orbicularis weakness.
Steroid side effects: Cataracts, Glaucoma, and Weight Gain must be monitored.
